questions.prompt: Which assertion tests behavior rather than implementation?
questions.explanation: total() is the public, observable contract; the others reach into private internals and break on refactors.

questions.prompt: Why are implementation-coupled tests called brittle 'change detectors'?

options.text: They fail on internal changes even when behavior is unchanged (false failures)
They run faster than behavior tests

questions.explanation: Coupled to internals, they go red on behavior-preserving refactors — false failures that discourage improving the code.

questions.prompt: The gut-check question: if you change the ____ without changing behavior, the test should still pass.
questions.explanation: If a behavior-preserving implementation change would break the test, the test is coupled to implementation and should be loosened.

questions.prompt: Which are warning signs of implementation-coupled tests? Select all that apply.

options.text: Asserting on private methods or private fields
Verifying the exact internal call sequence
Pinning incidental output ordering that isn't part of the contract

questions.explanation: Private internals, exact call order, and incidental details are coupling smells; asserting the public result is exactly right.

questions.prompt: Match each assertion target to its robustness/appropriateness.

pairs.right: High — when the effect is the behavior
Low — only if the interaction is the contract
Very low — usually a design smell

questions.explanation: Prefer results and observable effects; reserve interaction checks for genuine contracts and avoid private-detail assertions.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to turn a brittle test into a behavior test.

items.text: Spot the assertion on a private detail or call sequence
Identify the public behavior callers actually rely on
Assert that behavior through the public API

questions.explanation: Find the coupling, determine the real contract, and re-assert it through the public interface.
